elemental-composition-s1.title: Burning magnesium in three labs
elemental-composition-s1.text: Three lab groups heat different masses of pure magnesium in air until it has all turned into a white solid, magnesium oxide, and weigh the product.

table.caption: Mass of magnesium used and of magnesium oxide made

elemental-composition-s2.title: Analysis of a sweet-tasting compound
elemental-composition-s2.text: A lab analyzes a pure white solid that contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Its molar mass is found separately to be 180.2 g/mol.

items.q: What is the mass percent of magnesium in Group 1's product?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the oxygen share. Use the mass of magnesium on top.
Value: divide by the mass of the whole product (2.016 g), not by the oxygen alone.

items.q: Which conclusion do the three groups' results support?
options: Magnesium oxide is about 60.3% magnesium by mass in each sample
Larger samples of magnesium oxide contain a larger percent of magnesium
Magnesium and oxygen combine in a 1 : 1 ratio by mass
The groups made different compounds, since their product masses differ

why.correct: All three products are 60.3% Mg by mass. A compound has the same composition by mass whatever the sample size.
options: Right: 60.32%, 60.32% and 60.31%: a fixed composition, the law of definite proportions.
The masses differ, but the percent is the same in every group.
Group 1 used 1.216 g Mg with 0.800 g O, a mass ratio of about 1.5 : 1, not 1 : 1.
Different amounts of one compound have different masses but the same composition.

items.q: Using Group 2's data, what is the empirical formula of magnesium oxide?
options: Mg₃O₂
MgO₂
Mg₂O
MgO

why.correct: Formulas count atoms, so compare moles: 0.1251 mol Mg : 0.1250 mol O = 1 : 1, so MgO.
options: This uses the mass ratio, about 3 : 2, as if it were a ratio of atoms. Convert masses to moles first.
This would need twice as many moles of O as Mg; the moles are equal.
This would need twice as many moles of Mg as O; the moles are equal.

items.q: Based on the groups' results, what mass of magnesium is in 12.5 g of magnesium oxide?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the oxygen in the sample. Use the magnesium fraction, 0.6032.
Value: you divided by the fraction. The part is the whole times the fraction.

why.correct: Magnesium oxide is 60.32% Mg by mass: 12.5 g × 0.6032 = 7.54 g of Mg.

items.q: A fourth group's product had a magnesium mass percent of 66%. Which error best explains this result?
options: The group used more magnesium than the other groups
Some magnesium did not react, so the product was too light
The product absorbed water from the air after heating
The balance read each mass 0.05 g too high

why.correct: Mass percent Mg = mass Mg ÷ mass product. If the product is too light because not all Mg reacted with oxygen, the percent rises above the true 60.3%.
options: Sample size does not change the percent of a pure compound.
Right: too little oxygen gained makes the product too light, and the Mg share comes out too high.
Extra water would add mass and lower the Mg percent, not raise it.
A balance that reads every mass 0.05 g high moves the percent by only about 1 to 2 percentage points for these samples, not 6.

items.q: What is the empirical formula of the compound?
options: C₄₀H₇O₅₃
C₃H₇O₃
C₆H₁₂O₆
CH₂O
Percents are masses, not atom counts. Convert each to moles first.
This rounds the moles in 100 g (3.33, 6.66, 3.33) instead of dividing by the smallest.
That is the molecular formula; the empirical formula is the simplest ratio.
Right: per 100 g, 3.331 mol C, 6.657 mol H, 3.331 mol O; dividing by 3.331 gives 1 : 2 : 1.

items.q: What is the molar mass of the empirical formula CH₂O (one C, two H and one O)?
What is the molecular formula of the compound?
options: CH₂O
C₁₂H₂₄O₁₂
C₆H₁₂O₆
C₃H₆O₃

why.correct: n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass = 180.2 / 30.03 = 6. Multiply every subscript by 6: C₆H₁₂O₆.
options: The empirical formula has a molar mass of 30.03, not 180.2.
That is twelve CH₂O units, 360.3 g/mol, twice the molar mass measured.
Right: 180.2 ÷ 30.03 = 6.00, so the molecule is six CH₂O units.
This is three CH₂O units, with a molar mass of 90.08 g/mol.

items.q: Another compound has the same mass percents (40.00% C, 6.71% H, 53.29% O) but a molar mass of 60.05 g/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: It is the same compound, because the mass percents match
The data are wrong, since two compounds do not share mass percents
Its empirical formula is also CH₂O, and its molecular formula is C₂H₄O₂
Its molecular formula is CH₂O, since 60.05 is close to 30.03

why.correct: Mass percents fix only the empirical formula. The molar mass then sets the multiple: 60.05 ÷ 30.03 = 2, so C₂H₄O₂.
options: Matching percents show the same empirical formula, not the same molecule; the molar masses differ.
Many compounds share an empirical formula: CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆ have identical percents.
Right: same percents, same simplest ratio; 60.05 / 30.03 = 2.
60.05 is twice 30.03, so the molecule is two CH₂O units.

items.q: Urea, CH₄N₂O, is used as a fertilizer. What is the mass percent of nitrogen in urea? (C 12.01, H 1.008, N 14.01, O 16.00)

mistakes.why: Value: urea has two N atoms. Use 2 × 14.01 for the nitrogen mass.

items.q: A 2.233 g sample of iron reacts with oxygen to make 3.193 g of an iron oxide. What is the empirical formula of the oxide? (Fe 55.85, O 16.00)
options: FeO
FeO₂
Fe₃O₂
Fe₂O₃

why.correct: O gained = 3.193 − 2.233 = 0.960 g = 0.0600 mol. Fe = 2.233/55.85 = 0.03998 mol. O/Fe = 1.50; multiply both by 2: Fe₂O₃.
options: Oxygen and iron come out 1.5 : 1 in moles, not 1 : 1.
Oxygen and iron come out 1.5 : 1 in moles, not 2 : 1. Rounding 1.5 is not allowed; multiply to whole numbers instead.
This puts more iron than oxygen; the moles of O are larger.
Right: 0.03998 mol Fe and 0.0600 mol O, a ratio of 1 : 1.5, which doubles to 2 : 3.

items.q: Put the steps for finding an empirical formula from mass percents in order.
options: Assume a 100 g sample so each percent becomes grams
Divide each mass by its molar mass to get moles
Divide every mole value by the smallest one
Multiply by a small whole number if any ratio is not close to whole
Write the formula with the whole-number ratios as subscripts

why.correct: Percent → grams → moles → divide by the smallest → clear fractions → formula.

items.q: A student finds that elements X and Y are present in moles in the ratio 1 : 1.33 and writes the formula XY. What should the student have done?
options: Round 1.33 to 1, so XY is correct
Multiply both by 3 to get 3 : 4, so X₃Y₄
Multiply both by 2 to get 2 : 2.66, so X₂Y₃
Divide both by 1.33 to get 0.75 : 1, then round to XY

why.correct: Recognize common fractions: x.5 → ×2, x.33 or x.67 → ×3, x.25 or x.75 → ×4. 1 : 1.33 × 3 = 3 : 4.
options: A ratio 0.33 from a whole number is a real fraction, not rounding error.
Right: 1.33 is 4/3; multiplying by 3 clears the fraction.
2.66 is not close to a whole number; multiply by 3.
Dividing gives 0.75 : 1, and 0.75 is a real fraction, not rounding error; rounding it away loses the true ratio of 3 : 4.

items.q: A compound of only carbon and hydrogen has the empirical formula CH₂ (14.03 g/mol). Which could be its molecular formula? Select all that apply.
options: C₂H₄
C₃H₆
CH₄
C₂H₆

why.correct: A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so it keeps the 1 : 2 ratio.
options: Right: 2 × CH₂.
Right: 3 × CH₂.
The C : H ratio is 1 : 4, not 1 : 2.
The C : H ratio is 1 : 3, not 1 : 2.

items.q: Water and hydrogen peroxide both contain only hydrogen and oxygen. Water is 11.2% H by mass; hydrogen peroxide is 5.93% H. Which explains the difference?
options: They are different compounds, H₂O and H₂O₂, with different atom ratios
Hydrogen peroxide samples were less pure than the water samples
The law of definite proportions says compounds of two elements share a composition
Hydrogen atoms in the peroxide are lighter than the hydrogen atoms in water

why.correct: Different ratios of the same atoms make different compounds, each with its own fixed mass percents: H₂O 2.016/18.02 = 11.2% H; H₂O₂ 2.016/34.01 = 5.93% H.
options: Right: each compound has its own fixed composition; peroxide has more O per H.
Each percent is fixed for its own pure compound, so contamination is not the cause.
The law says each compound has a fixed composition, not that different compounds share one.
Every H atom has the same average mass; the number of O atoms per H differs.

items.q: A compound is 26.58% K, 35.35% Cr and 38.07% O by mass. What is its empirical formula? (K 39.10, Cr 52.00, O 16.00)
options: KCrO₃
KCrO₄
K₂Cr₂O₇
K₂CrO₄
This rounds 3.5 down to 3; a ratio of x.5 must be doubled.
This rounds 3.5 up to 4; a ratio of x.5 must be doubled.
Right: moles 0.6798 : 0.6798 : 2.379 = 1 : 1 : 3.5, and doubling gives 2 : 2 : 7.
K and Cr come out 1 : 1 in moles, so their subscripts must be equal.
